-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 1 - PURPOSE AND KEY CONCEPTS
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.1 What this insurance does

Combined residential buildings insurance protects the policyholder against the
financial consequences of physical damage to their building. The perils that can
be insured are the ones bundled together in these conditions - fire, escape of
water, storm and hail, and further natural hazards among them. Which of the
insurable perils are actually covered, and which of the optional extensions
apply, is agreed between insurer and policyholder and recorded in the schedule.

Where insured property is destroyed or damaged, the insurer indemnifies the cost
of putting it back, on an index-linked reinstatement basis with an enhancement.
A range of consequential expenses triggered by a loss event is also carried,
within the limits agreed for each head.

Two distinctions run through the whole of this wording. The first is between the
escape that causes a loss and the damage that escape causes: damage to insured
property is indemnified even where the installation from which the water escaped
is not itself insured property, while putting that installation back into working
order is a separate matter governed by 2.4.4, 4.4.2 and 7.1.8. The second is
between the parts and items the loss actually reached and those it did not: the
first are made good, the second are not, however sensible it may be to treat them
at the same time.

1.2 How the wording is to be read

Personal designations are to be understood as gender-neutral throughout; no
parallel male and female forms are used.

1.3 Explanation of recurring terms (not legally binding)

Policyholder - the insurer's contracting party and the purchaser of the cover.

Insured event - the event for which the insurer pays.

Exclusion - a peril, a type of damage or an item of property for which no cover
exists. Exclusions delimit what has been promised and keep the cover calculable.

Affected part or item - a room, surface, building component, finish, fitting,
installation or furnishing on which physical damage caused by the insured event
is established by the loss investigation - by inspection, by photographic record,
by technical measurement or by a technical report - taken at or shortly after the
time of the loss. An item on which no such damage is established is not an
affected item, whatever its proximity to the affected ones and whatever the risk
that it might have been reached.

Source installation - the pipe, vessel, plant or equipment from which the water
escaped, whether or not it is insured property.

Repair cost - the outlay directed at making good the physical damage caused by
the insured event on an affected part or item. Outlay that pursues any other
purpose is not a repair cost, however it may be described or invoiced.

Ancillary charge - any charge raised alongside the itemised labour and materials:
call-out and travel, carriage, delivery, disposal, administration, handling and
comparable items.

Optional extension - a widening of the cover which applies only where it is
recorded in the schedule. Where an extension is not recorded, the base wording
applies unchanged.

Duties - the things the policyholder must do or refrain from doing before, during
and after an insured event.

Secured lenders - creditors whose claim is secured by a charge registered against
the property. The interests of secured lenders enjoy statutory protection.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 2 - INSURED PERILS
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2.1 The perils that can be covered

The insurer indemnifies insured property that is destroyed or damaged by, or lost
as a consequence of, the following events:

  (a) FIRE GROUP - fire; lightning strike; overvoltage caused by lightning;
      explosion; deflagration; implosion; impact or crash of an aircraft, its
      parts or its cargo; impact of a vehicle; scorching; smoke and soot.

  (b) ESCAPE OF WATER.

  (c) NATURAL HAZARDS, in two tiers:
        (c1) storm and hail;
        (c2) the further natural hazards - flood, backing-up of water,
             earthquake, ground subsidence, landslip, snow load, avalanche and
             volcanic eruption.

2.2 How the groups combine

Each of the three groups (a), (b) and (c1) can be taken separately. The further
natural hazards under (c2) can only be taken in combination with one or more of
the perils in (a), (b) or (c1).

2.3 The fire group defined

2.3.1 Fire is a combustion that has started without a hearth intended for it, or
that has escaped such a hearth, and that is capable of spreading under its own
power. Lightning strike is the direct passage of a lightning discharge onto
property. Overvoltage caused by lightning covers damage through overvoltage,
overcurrent or short circuit in insured electrical installations and appliances.

2.3.2 Explosion and deflagration are suddenly running force events resting on the
tendency of gases or vapours to expand; implosion is a sudden collapse of a
hollow body under external overpressure.

2.3.3 The impact or crash of an aircraft, its parts or its cargo is covered, as
is the impact of a road, rail or water-borne vehicle, save where its keeper or
driver is the policyholder or an occupant of the building.

2.3.4 Scorch damage arising out of one of the events above is covered; scorch
damage from any other cause up to [amount]. Smoke and soot damage arising out of
one of those events is covered; damage from the gradual action of smoke or soot
is not.

2.3.5 Not covered within this group is damage caused by earthquake; damage to
internal combustion engines from explosions inside the combustion chamber; and
damage at the switching elements of electrical switches from the gas pressure
inside them, unless the consequence of an insured fire event.

2.4 Escape of water defined

2.4.1 The three headings
The escape of water peril covers three things: damage caused by escaping water;
fracture damage to insured pipework inside buildings; and fracture damage to
insured pipework outside buildings.

2.4.2 Damage caused by escaping water
Escaping water means water that has emerged, contrary to its intended purpose,
from a water-carrying installation situated on the insured site. It is immaterial
for this heading whether the source installation is itself insured property,
whether it belongs to the building or to a separate facility on the site, and
whether the water it carried was drawn from the mains supply or held in a basin,
tank or circuit.

Covered under this heading is the damage the escaping water causes to insured
property: the wetting, soaking, staining, swelling, distortion, detachment,
corrosion, contamination and comparable physical impairment of the affected
rooms, surfaces, components, finishes, fittings, installations and furnishings,
together with the consequential damage arising from it. The path the water took
determines the extent of the cover: rooms into which the water ran, and the parts
and items within them that it reached, are covered wherever they lie on that
path, including ancillary and plant rooms.

Operating fluids from heating, air-conditioning, circulation and treatment
systems, and steam, also count as escaping water. Fluids intended for the
generation of energy do not.

2.4.3 Fracture damage to insured pipework
Covered inside buildings is frost-related and other fracture damage to the pipes
of the water and gas supply, of heating and air-conditioning systems, of
water-based extinguishing and sprinkler systems and of rainwater drainage,
together with frost-related fracture damage to the sanitary fittings, valves,
radiators, boilers and comparable parts of those systems. Covered outside
buildings is frost-related and other fracture damage to supply pipes of the water
supply and to pipes of heating or air-conditioning systems, insofar as the
policyholder bears the risk for them and insofar as they serve the supply of
insured buildings or are situated on the insured site.

This heading presupposes in every case that the pipework concerned is insured
property under Part 4.

Putting the source installation back into working order is not part of the
indemnity under 2.4.2.

Where the source installation is insured property - because it falls within 2.4.3
or because an optional extension under 4.4.2 applies to it - its repair is
indemnified under 2.4.3, together with the labour, components, fittings,
connections and sealing materials belonging to that repair.

Where the source installation is not insured property, neither its repair nor the
skilled or unskilled labour, the components, fittings, connections, sealing,
refilling, recommissioning or functional testing belonging to that repair is
indemnified, however plainly its failure caused the covered damage, on whichever
invoice those items appear, and by whichever trade they are billed.

Locating the escape, and establishing where the water went and what it wetted,
falls under 5.2.2 in either case and is not affected by the status of the source
installation.

2.4.5 Exclusions within this peril
Damage caused by the following is not covered, irrespective of any contributing
causes except where named: splash or cleaning water; dry rot and house-rot fungi
of every kind; groundwater, standing or flowing surface water, flood,
precipitation, or a backing-up brought about by any of these; earthquake, snow
load, avalanche, volcanic eruption; ground subsidence or landslip, unless
escaping water within the meaning of 2.4.2 caused it; the perils of the fire
group; the opening of sprinklers on account of fire, pressure testing or works;
storm or hail. Damage to buildings or parts of buildings that are not ready for
occupation is not covered.

2.5 Natural hazards defined

2.5.1 Storm means a weather-driven movement of air reaching at least the gale
threshold on the recognised scale of wind strength; hail means solid
precipitation in the form of grains of ice. Only damage arising from the direct
action of storm or hail on insured property, on buildings in which insured
property is located, or on buildings structurally joined to them, is covered,
together with damage caused by objects thrown onto them.

2.5.2 The further natural hazards are flood, backing-up of water, earthquake,
ground subsidence, landslip, snow load, avalanche and volcanic eruption, each as
customarily defined.

2.5.3 Not covered is damage caused by storm surge; by the penetration of
precipitation or dirt through openings that were not properly closed; by
groundwater save where it emerged at the surface as a result of precipitation or
overflow; by the perils of the fire group, save where triggered by an insured
earthquake; and by drought or desiccation.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PART 3 - EXCLUSIONS
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

3.1 General exclusions

3.1.1 War
Damage caused by war, warlike events, civil war, revolution, rebellion or
insurrection is not covered, irrespective of any contributing causes.

3.1.2 Civil commotion
Damage caused by internal civil unrest is not covered, irrespective of any
contributing causes.

3.1.3 Nuclear energy
Damage caused by nuclear energy, nuclear radiation or radioactive substances is
not covered, irrespective of any contributing causes.

3.1.4 Liability risks
Claims of third parties against the policyholder, and any outlay directed at
covering, assessing, administering or settling such claims, are not the subject
of this contract.

3.1.5 Upkeep, servicing and inspection of installations
Outlay directed at the servicing, maintenance, cleaning, adjustment, periodic
testing, certification or general condition of an installation is not
indemnifiable. This applies irrespective of whether the measure was performed on
the occasion of an insured event, was recommended in its aftermath, or was
carried out by a trade that also performed covered work.

This clause does not affect the measures described in 7.1.7, which are directed
at parts and items the loss actually reached and at their return to service.
Where an installation that is insured property was itself reached by the escaping
water, the examination, cleaning, flushing, drying, making good and
recommissioning of that installation necessitated by the ingress are treated as
making good under 7.1.7 and not as upkeep under this clause.

3.1.6 Precautionary and preventive measures
Renewing, replacing or upgrading a part or item on which no damage from the
insured event has been established is not indemnifiable, even where the measure
is taken as a precaution, on a technical recommendation, because the part or item
stands next to or in the same room as an affected one, or because a later failure
is thought possible. Establishing whether such a part or item was reached falls
under 5.2.2 and 7.1.7(g); replacing it where it was not falls under this clause.

3.2 Exclusions within the fire group

See 2.3.5.

3.3 Exclusions within the escape of water peril

See 2.4.4 and 2.4.5.

3.4 Exclusions within the natural hazards

See 2.5.3.

3.5 Work beyond the affected parts, and outlay that is not a repair cost

Work carried out beyond those parts and items of the insured property that were
themselves affected by the insured event is not covered. Outlay that does not
constitute a repair cost is not indemnified. The delimitation in each case is
governed by 7.1.5 to 7.1.10.

4.2 The categories defined

4.2.1 Building and dwelling

levelling layers; wall and ceiling finishes; interior doors; and fixed trim,
skirting, beading and comparable edging elements.

4.2.3 Building accessories and furnishings
Movable items located inside the building which serve the upkeep of the insured
building or its predominant intended purpose, together with the loose furnishings
of the affected rooms insofar as this is agreed in the schedule. Recreational,
decorative, horticultural and comparable loose articles - among them the
equipment, floats, covers and toys belonging to a water feature, and planters,
pots, plants and their contents - are not building accessories and are not
insured property.

4.2.4 Building services installations
The electrical, water, heating, air-conditioning, ventilation and comparable
technical installations serving the building are insured property insofar as they
serve the building itself and are not excluded under 4.3.

4.2.5 Terraces and further site installations
Terraces are paved surfaces intended for occupation in the open air. Further site
installations are the items firmly connected with the ground and soil of the
insured site listed in the schedule.

4.3 Property not insured

Not insured:
  (a) photovoltaic installations and their components, including a permanently

The exclusion of an installation under this clause does not exclude the damage

recommissioning, and every measure directed at it as such.

4.4 Optional extensions

4.4.1 Items subsequently incorporated by a tenant or condominium owner, and the
loose furnishings of the insured rooms, can be co-insured where this is agreed.

4.4.2 Water features and their technical plant
By way of departure from 4.3(b), a water feature situated on the insured site

  (a) the feature and its plant are insured property for all purposes of these

4.5 The insured location

The insured location is the insured site: the land parcel or parcels on which the
insured building stands.

4.6 Condominium and part-ownership units

Where the contract is with an association of condominium owners and the insurer
is wholly or partly released from liability on account of the conduct of
individual owners, it remains obliged to pay the remaining owners in respect of
their separate property and their shares in the common property. The remaining
owners may claim indemnity for the co-ownership share concerned where the
additional indemnity is applied to reinstating the common property; the owner
concerned must reimburse the insurer. These provisions apply correspondingly to
part-ownership units.

4.7 Deductibles

A deductible is the share of the indemnity, or the amount, that the policyholder

The insurer reimburses the following costs where they were necessary as a
consequence of an insured event and were actually incurred:
  (a) emergency and mitigation measures, including the extraction, pumping and
      removal of escaped water and the securing of the affected rooms;
  (b) locating the escape and establishing the extent of the wetting;
  (c) debris removal and disposal costs;
  (d) costs of moving and protecting property;
  (e) costs of lost water, gas and heating oil, and of electricity lost from
      storage installations;
  (f) hotel costs;
  (g) costs of returning early from a holiday.

Reimbursement of each of these heads is limited to the amount agreed for it.

5.2 The cost heads defined

5.2.1 Emergency and mitigation measures
Costs of the measures taken during or immediately after the insured event to end
the escape, to remove the water that has escaped and to prevent the damage from
increasing, capped at [amount] per insured event. Shutting off, isolating or
temporarily closing the source installation counts as such a measure; repairing
it is governed by 2.4.4.

5.2.2 Locating the escape and establishing the extent of the wetting

determine which rooms, surfaces, components and installations it reached and how
far they are wetted - moisture measurement, surveying, mapping, technical
reporting and comparable investigation - together with the follow-up measurements
needed to establish that the drying is complete. These costs are reimbursed
whether or not the source installation is insured property, whether the search
runs from the room where the damage showed to the room where the escape began,
and whether they are billed by the trade that carries out the drying or by
another.

5.2.3 Debris removal and disposal
Costs incurred in clearing away, removing and disposing of the material taken out
in the course of the covered works, including transport to the nearest disposal
site and the disposal charge itself. This head is reimbursed once per insured
event for the material concerned; a further charge for the same removal on the
invoice of another trade falls under 7.1.8(f).

5.2.4 Moving and protecting property
Costs incurred in moving, altering or protecting property, where those measures
serve to reinstate or replace insured property.

5.2.5 Lost water, gas, heating oil and stored electricity
Costs arising because these escaped or were lost contrary to their intended
purpose as a result of an insured event, capped at [amount] per insured event.
The cost of refilling an installation excluded under 4.3 does not fall under this
head.

5.2.6 Hotel costs
Costs of accommodation where the dwelling permanently occupied by the
policyholder has become uninhabitable and confining themselves to a habitable
part of it cannot reasonably be expected, reimbursed only to the extent that they
exceed the indemnity payable for rental value and only where indemnity cannot be
claimed under another insurance contract, up to [amount] per day for a maximum of
[number] days.

5.2.7 Early return from holiday
Additional travel costs arising because the policyholder, or a person living with
them in the same household, breaks off a holiday trip prematurely on account of a
significant insured event, in a reasonable amount and capped at [amount] per
insured event.

5.3 Loss of rent and rental value

The insurer reimburses loss of rent where tenants of residential premises have
lawfully stopped paying rent or terminated the tenancy on account of an insured
event, and the locally customary rental value of residential premises occupied by
the policyholder itself where use cannot reasonably be expected, in each case
including the running service charges in the sense of tenancy law.

5.4 The period for loss of rent and rental value

Loss of rent or rental value is reimbursed for the period during which the rooms
are unusable, but for no longer than [number] months from the occurrence of the
insured event, and only to the extent that the policyholder has not culpably
delayed the resumption of use.

5.5 Commercially used premises

For commercially used premises, insurance of loss of rent or of the locally
customary rental value can be agreed.

# Claim to Fame shortcuts.  Usage:
#   make 7             play game 7 (start it a few seconds before the game opens)
#   make play G=7      same thing
#   make check         real model against the permanent test game 0 (needs an LLM key in .env)

=== submit.sh ===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Submit prices for a game.
# Usage:  ./submit.sh GAME_ID 'INDEX:CHARGE:LIMIT' ['INDEX:CHARGE:LIMIT' ...]
#    or:  ./submit.sh GAME_ID path/to/submissions.json
# Example: ./submit.sh 0 1:410:430 2:120:150
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
GAME_ID="${1:?usage: ./submit.sh GAME_ID 'IDX:A:B' ... | file.json}"; shift
BASE_URL="https://c2f.public.quantco.cloud"

if [[ -z "${TEAM_API_KEY:-}" && -f .env ]]; then
  TEAM_API_KEY="$(grep -E '^TEAM_API_KEY=' .env | cut -d= -f2- | tr -d '"'"'" )"
fi
[[ -n "${TEAM_API_KEY:-}" ]] || { echo "TEAM_API_KEY not set (env or .env)"; exit 1; }

if [[ $# -eq 1 && -f "$1" ]]; then
  BODY="$(cat "$1")"
else
  items=()
  for spec in "$@"; do
    IFS=: read -r idx a b <<<"$spec"
    items+=("{\"index\":$idx,\"charge_price\":$a,\"acceptance_limit\":$b}")
  done
  BODY="[$(IFS=,; echo "${items[*]}")]"
fi

echo "PUT $BASE_URL/api/games/$GAME_ID/submissions"
echo "$BODY"
curl -s -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' -X PUT \
  -H "X-API-Key: $TEAM_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "$BODY" "$BASE_URL/api/games/$GAME_ID/submissions"

content.text:
Game 2 opened 13:12:37 and was already `completed` by 13:15:42. The window is ~1 minute as the brief states. Our game-1 run at 13:06 was never going to land.

## Why we lost game 1

**Two independent failures. Either one alone loses the round.**

**1. The run started 6m09s late.** Game 1 opened 13:00:00Z; `started_at` in your log is 13:06:09Z. The fast answer was ready at +394s and the full at +404s, against a ~60s window. Even with submitting enabled, both would have been rejected as late.

**2. `--no-submit` was passed.** Both entries record `"skipped (--no-submit)"`. This wasn't a tooling default — `make 1` submits, and the flag is opt-in at `c2f/run.py:86`. It was explicit on that invocation.

So the server applied defaults `a=0, b=0`.

## Where the −8,273.70 came from

| side | what happened | result |
|---|---|---|
| issuer | `a=0` on all 18 items × 16 opponents | 288 transactions "accepted", income **€0** |
| insurer | `b=0` rejected all 45 non-zero incoming charges | 27 were **fair** → paid 1.5a each |

Σ of those 27 charges = 5,515.80; × 1.5 = **8,273.70** exactly. The other 18 were genuinely fraudulent and correctly rejected at zero cost. The remaining 243 opponents also charged 0.

Thirteen of seventeen teams share that exact score — it is the "submitted nothing" signature, not a strategy failure.

## What the values you computed were actually worth

Scored against provable ground truth only (charges the engine confirmed as fair, so `t ≥ a`):

| | insurer cost | guaranteed income | net |
|---|---|---|---|
| actual (defaults) | 8,273.70 | 0 | **−8,273.70** |
| your `full` / gpt-5 | 6,806.74 | 27,552 | **≥ +20,745** |
| your `fast` / gpt-5-mini | 6,215.15 | 11,420 | **≥ +5,205** |

Those income figures are *lower bounds* — they count only 7 of 18 items, the ones where our `a` sits below a proven `t`. Fair charges are paid by every opponent regardless of their limit, so that money was certain.

The miss cost roughly **29,000**, against a first place of 33,436. The pipeline was good enough to win game 1.

## Two genuine model errors, worth fixing

**Item 18** — "premium hardwood skirting boards (upgrade from pre-loss softwood)". Both models set `t=0` because it's an upgrade. Proven `t ≥ 98.02`. The *upgrade* isn't covered, but the like-for-like softwood replacement is: an upgrade line is worth **the pre-loss-standard equivalent, not zero**. Same applies to item 4 (stone-for-ceramic, charged 1728 with `b=0`). That's a systematic, generalisable prompt fix.

**Item 1** — "clean / dry conservatory rug". gpt-5 ruled it not covered (loose furnishing, 4.2.3) and set `b=0`; proven `t ≥ 122.94`. gpt-5-mini had it covered at `t_mid=120` and was right. Note this one is *confident and wrong*, so a continuous `p_valid` wouldn't have saved it — 0.5 is still below the ⅔ bar. Model disagreement is the signal here, not uncertainty within one model.

Broader exposure: `full` set `b=0` on 8 of 18 items. Each wrong `b=0` pays 1.5a to all 16 opponents.

## Correction to something I told you earlier

I said there's no results endpoint and per-item threshold learning was impossible. **That was wrong.** The leaderboard has undocumented endpoints — `/leaderboard/api/{performance,matrix,matchup,transactions,games}` — and `transactions` gives per-matchup outcomes. Game 1 alone yields 27 exact lower bounds on `t`. The Branch A learning design is available after all, and `docs/DESIGN.md` §13 needs correcting.

## The fix that actually matters

Not "remember the flag". 100 games, one every ~12.6 minutes, each with a ~60-second window. The Makefile comment says *"start it a few seconds before the game opens"* — a manual protocol that will miss rounds. This needs a scheduler that polls `/api/games`, wakes before each `start_time`, runs, and submits — plus the T+8 safety-net submission so a slow model still produces something.

Game 3 opens at **13:25:15Z**. Not submitting anything, per your instruction — tell me when you want that scheduler built.

Now it's clear. Answer to your question, in order of what actually matters:

## Is the mathematical model wired?

Wired and verified end to end, but it had **never once run on real model output** until just now — and doing so exposed a bug that had been silently corrupting it.

`extract_json` scanned for `{` before `[`, so on a JSON *array* it returned only the first object. On the 18-item case that meant **item 1 got real inference and items 2–18 all fell back to the heuristic** — with no error logged. That's why my case-1 run showed 15 identical rows. Fixed, with a regression test that asserts on the *last* array element rather than the first. 126 tests pass.

Also: `LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic` with an empty key, so every call failed and degraded. Your OpenAI key works — I ran through it with `LLM_PROVIDER=openai LLM_MODEL=gpt-5-mini`. That needs to become the default in `.env` or the pipeline is dead weight.

## Your model vs mine: same LLM, two maths

I fed both pricing functions the **identical** gpt-5-mini beliefs from your game-1 log. The `b` values come out nearly the same (112.05 vs 112.54, 168.08 vs 168.99) — both implement the same ⅓-quantile rule, so `b` is not a differentiator at all. The only difference is `a`, and mine is higher on every line.

Scored against where `t` actually sits:

| strategy | t = proven bound | t ≥ t_mid |
|---|---|---|
| yours, K=0.5 (current) | **12,785** | 38,625 |
| yours, K=0.25 (before) | 5,205 | **48,505** |
| mine, μ=1.0 | 4,989 | **47,818** |
| mine, μ=0.85 | 3,113 | 39,518 |

**The decision math is not where the money is.** Your K=0.25 and my optimiser land within 1.5% of each other. Once the shading matches, the two formulas are equivalent in practice. My design's edge isn't a better formula — it's that `mu_shift` is a *fitted* parameter rather than a hand-tuned constant, and we finally have data to fit it.

## The finding you should act on

You raised `K_UNCERTAINTY` from 0.25 to 0.5 because game 2 looked like ~15% over-pricing. **Game 1's data says the opposite.** Of 8 items where `t` is measurable, 5 have `t` *strictly above* `t_mid`:

| item | t_mid | proven t ≥ | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 9 | 260 | 409.79 | ≥1.58 |
| 7 | 130 | 182.13 | ≥1.40 |
| 2, 13 | 180 | 227.66 | ≥1.26 |
| 1 | 120 | 122.94 | ≥1.02 |

Zero items show evidence of over-estimation — the other three just have weak bounds. Median lower bound on `t/t_mid` is 1.14. In that regime, K=0.5 costs about **10,000 per round** versus K=0.25.

Caveat worth stating: these bounds come from other teams' charges that were ruled fair, so they're valid lower bounds but a biased-low estimate of `t`. The direction of the bias only strengthens the conclusion — real `t` is at least this high.

Game 2 has completed, so the same analysis is available for it. That's the honest way to settle K: fit it on both rounds rather than reacting to one.

## Ranked by euros

1. **Submit at all** — ~29,000/round. Two independent failures in game 1 (6 minutes late, `--no-submit`).
2. **Stop over-shading `a`** — ~10,000/round. Revert K to 0.25, or fit `mu_shift` from transaction data.
3. **Upgrade lines aren't worth zero** — item 18 proved `t ≥ 98` where both models said 0. An upgrade is worth the pre-loss-standard equivalent.
4. The pricing formula itself — worth ~1.5%. Not the priority.

content.text:
Now I can answer that precisely, and the answer is encouraging.

## error404's lead is a one-off, not a trend

| | game 1 | game 2 | game 3 | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| error404 ai | **33,436** | 4,803 | 403 | 38,642 |
| AsianSuperNerds | −8,274 | **11,651** | 0 | 3,377 |

**87% of their total is game 1** — the round where 13 of 17 teams submitted nothing and their fair charges collected `a` from everyone plus the 1.5× penalty. That cannot repeat now the field is awake.

Since everyone woke up: **games 2+3, we scored 11,651 to their 5,206.** We were #1 in game 2, ahead of Codacabana's 10,355. The 35,265 gap closes at roughly 3,200/game at that differential, so ~11 rounds, with ~97 left.

## What won us game 2

Income 14,215, insurer cost 2,564 → net 11,651. Two correct fair charges produced 97% of it:

| item | our charge | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 555.00 | fair → paid by all 16 = 8,880 |
| 1 | 310.00 | fair → paid by all 16 = 4,960 |
| 2,3,5,6,7 | 12–60 | fraud → 2–3 lenient reviewers each = 375 |

error404 only priced item 4 and charged **525.35** where we charged **555** — both fair, so `t ≥ 555`. Their shading cost them 475 on that one item. That's direct empirical confirmation of the `K=0.5` finding: on the one item where we can measure it, charging *less* lost money.

## Your insurer side is already solved

Cumulative: **0 wrongfully accepted, and all 27 wrongful rejections were game 1's `b=0`.** Games 2 and 3 had zero of each — perfect classification. Insurer cost fell from 8,274 to 2,564. Don't touch `b`; it's doing exactly what the ⅔ rule promises. Every remaining euro is on `a`.

## The one thing game 3 exposes

Game 3 was two items, `t` very low on both. We charged above every opponent's limit and earned **0**. error404 charged ~101 and ~100, got rejected by 14, and **2 lenient reviewers paid each → 403 at zero risk.**

We know our low free-shots work — in game 2 our 12–60 charges caught 2–3 acceptors apiece. So game 3 wasn't a strategy failure, it was a *level* failure: `a = 0.6 × t_if_covered` scales with the item's hypothetical value, which on an expensive-but-worthless item lands far above anyone's limit.

The fix is to aim the free shot at the lenient tail rather than at a fraction of the item's value. Two of sixteen teams accept around €100, so on a believed-worthless item the charge should sit near that, regardless of what the item would have cost if covered. That's the `argmax a·G(a)` term — and we now have three rounds of transaction data to fit `G` from.

Priorities unchanged in rank, updated in size: never miss a round; stop over-shading fair charges (`K` back to 0.25); cap the free-shot at the observed lenient-acceptance level rather than scaling it with item value.

content.text:
Careful — that question conflates two different situations, and the answers point in opposite directions.

**When we *believe* `t` is low**, `a` already scales down automatically: `argmax a·S(a)` is proportional to our median. Nothing to change.

**When we believe the item is worthless** (`t ≈ 0`), `S(a) ≈ 0` for every positive `a`, so the objective collapses to `a·G(a)` — pure opponent acceptance. The item's hypothetical value drops out of the maths entirely, which is exactly why `a = 0.6 × t_if_covered` is the wrong rule. But whether that means *lower* depends on the shape of `G`. Let me measure it rather than guess:

The curve is the key finding, and it's the **opposite** of the intuition:

`G(a)` barely decays — 0.167 at €17 down to only 0.062 at €512, a 2.7× fall across a 30× price range. So `a·G(a)` rises monotonically: **2.83 → 5.00 → 6.57 → 14.00 → 17.11 → 32.03**. There's a stubborn ~6–12% of reviewers who accept almost anything.

Now I can answer properly, with error bars.

## No — and in fact the opposite, but stop scaling it with the item's value

Two separate mistakes, in opposite directions:

**Game 2: our free shots were too LOW.** We charged €12–60 on the five worthless items and collected €375. At those levels `a·G(a)` is 2.83–6.57 per opponent; at €100–200 it's **14.00**. Same zero risk, roughly triple the return.

**Game 3: our free shots were too HIGH.** Nobody accepted, so we collected nothing — our charges sat above even the most lenient reviewer's limit.

Both follow from the same root cause: `a = 0.6 × t_if_covered` ties the charge to the item's hypothetical value, which is the one quantity that provably does **not** affect the answer. When `S(a) ≈ 0`, revenue is `a·G(a)`, and `G` is a property of *opponents*, not of the item.

## Where the honest uncertainty is

Censoring rate is 24.5% — a charge nobody accepted leaves no record of its size, and big charges are the likeliest to be refused by everyone. So the curve is optimistic exactly where the sample is thinnest:

| band | observations | `a·G(a)` |
|---|---|---|
| 0–25 | 3 | 2.83 |
| 25–50 | 9 | 5.00 |
| 50–100 | 6 | 6.57 |
| **100–200** | **12** | **14.00** |
| 200–400 | 1 | 17.11 |
| 400+ | 2 | 46.27 optimistic / **12.62** worst-case |

Under the worst case — every censored charge sitting in the top band — 400+ drops *below* the 100–200 band. So the evidence supports charging up to about **€100–200 flat** and does not support going beyond it. That is precisely where error404 sat in game 3 (€100.40 and €101.32), collecting 403 at zero risk while we collected nothing.

## Concrete rule

On an item believed worthless: `b = 0` (unchanged), and `a` ≈ €120–150 **flat**, regardless of `t_if_covered`. Revisit the band as censoring resolves — every round adds observations, and `argmax a·G(a)` should eventually be fit rather than hand-set.

## Keep it in proportion

Fixing this is worth roughly **+750/round** (five worthless items × ~224 each, versus the 375 we actually got). Compare: game 2's two correct fair charges produced **13,840**. So this is a real free improvement, but it's second-order — do it after never missing a round and after reverting `K` to 0.25.

One forward risk worth noting: the transaction feed names issuers, so opponents can profile us. A team that always charges €150 on junk lines is easy to filter out, and `G` will shrink as the field learns. That argues for fitting `G` continuously rather than fixing a constant now.

content.text:
Both modules already exist and do real work — `truth.py` recovers `t` intervals from the matchup equations (both bounds, stronger than the lower bounds I was computing by hand), and `feedback.py` extracts every team's charges plus implied `b` bounds. So the learning *inputs* exist; nothing feeds them back into pricing yet.

Here is the model as it actually stands.

## 1. Estimating `t` — a distribution, never a point

**Stage 1, LLM votes.** Three gpt-5 calls in parallel, each seeing policy + description + invoice verbatim. Per line item each returns `covered`, `related`, the clause cited, and a triple `(t_low, t_mid, t_high)` — its belief about the gross total a frugal claims expert would still accept. If not covered: all zero plus `t_if_covered`.

**Stage 2, aggregation** (`ensemble.py`): `covered` by majority, a tie counting as *not* covered. `t_low/t_mid/t_high` = median over the votes that said covered. That median is the only place model disagreement gets absorbed.

**Stage 3, representation.** The triple becomes a **triangular density on `[t_low, t_high]` with mode `t_mid`**. That is the belief about `t`, and everything downstream reads only from it.

The CDF is closed-form, which is why the triangle was chosen:

```
F(x) = (x−lo)² / ((hi−lo)(mode−lo))            x ≤ mode
     = 1 − (hi−x)² / ((hi−lo)(hi−mode))        x > mode
```

## 2. `b` — derived from the payoff table, not tuned

Facing a charge `a`, with `p = P(t ≥ a)`:

- accept → pay `a`
- reject → pay `1.5a` with probability `p` (it was fair), `0` otherwise

So `E[reject] = 1.5a·p`, and accepting is better exactly when

```
a ≤ 1.5·a·p    ⟺    p ≥ 2/3
```

Therefore `b = sup{a : P(t ≥ a) ≥ 2/3}`, i.e. the value where `F(b) = 1/3` — the **⅓-quantile of the belief**:

```python
b = tri_quantile(t_low, t_mid, t_high, 1/3)
  = lo + sqrt((1/3)·(hi−lo)·(mid−lo))          # when that lands below the mode
```

Not covered → `b = 0`, because then `P(t ≥ a) = 0 < 2/3` for every positive `a`.

The ⅓ is **not a tunable constant** — it falls out of the 1.5 penalty. Both engines derive it independently and agree. Empirically it's been flawless: 0 wrongfully accepted and 0 wrongfully rejected across games 2 and 3.

## 3. `a` — this is the heuristic half

**Live formula** (`price.py`):

```python
spread = (t_high − t_low) / t_mid
a = max(t_low, t_mid · (1 − K·spread))      K = 0.5
a = 0.6 · t_if_covered                       # when not covered
```

That is a hand-tuned downward shade off the mode. It is *not* derived from the payoff table, and `K` and `0.6` are free parameters set by eye.

**My engine's formula** (`decision/optimizer.py`) derives it instead. From the payoff table's left column, a fair charge is paid whether or not the insurer accepts — so the opponent's limit only matters above `t`:

```
R(a) = a·S(a)  +  min(a,c)·(1 − S(a))·G(a)        S(a) = P(t ≥ a)
       └ fair: paid by everyone ┘   └ fraud: only lenient reviewers ┘

a* = argmax R(a)      over 2000 log-spaced points in [0.02·q50, 4·q50]
```

With no opponent model this is `argmax a·S(a)`, which for a lognormal belief solves `hazard(z) = σ` — landing near the 24th percentile at `σ=0.4` and near the 72nd at `σ=1.2`. Uncertainty pushes `a` *up*, which is the opposite of what the `K·spread` shade does.

When the item is worthless, `S(a) ≈ 0` and it collapses to `argmax a·G(a)` — no dependence on the item's value at all.

My belief representation differs too: a 5-knot ladder `q10…q90` interpolated in `log(price)` with lognormal tails, under a hurdle model — `t = 0` with probability `1 − p_valid`, else drawn from the positive part — so `S(a) = p_valid · (1 − F₊(a))`.

## 4. What is fitted, and what is guessed

| quantity | status |
|---|---|
| `B_QUANTILE = 1/3` | **derived** from the payoff table |
| `t_low/t_mid/t_high` | LLM ensemble median |
| `K = 0.5` | **hand-set**, and the data says it's wrong (5 of 8 measurable items had `t > t_mid`) |
| `UNCOVERED_CHARGE = 0.6` | **hand-set**, and provably the wrong functional form — the value it scales by doesn't enter the objective |
| `mu_shift`, `sigma_scale` | exist in my models, currently 1.0, never fitted |
| `G(a)` | measured offline; not wired into pricing |

So the honest summary: **`b` is a theorem and it's working. `t` is an LLM ensemble median. `a` is two hand-tuned constants, and both are the things currently costing money** — `K` at roughly 10,000/round, `UNCOVERED_CHARGE` at roughly 750/round.

`truth.py` already recovers the `t` intervals needed to fit `mu_shift` properly, and `feedback.py` already recovers the acceptance data needed to fit `G`. The missing piece is only the loop that closes them back into `price.py`.

This also covers most of what the strategy write-up needs, if you want me to turn it into that.

content.text:
Good — with `runs/` and `truth_game_*.json` local, the calibration loop has everything it needs. One fix first: my script mislabelled item 1 as "worthless". It isn't — `t ≥ 199.25` means it *is* covered. I'll treat it as undetermined below.

## The one hidden number

Each line has a secret ceiling `t`: the most a fair expert would sign off. Everything is a bet on which side of it your price sits.

## You play both sides, and they're lopsided in opposite directions

**As the handyman you cannot lose money.** Worst case, nobody pays you. There is no penalty for asking too much.

**As the insurer you cannot make money.** Best case, you pay the fair price.

So the whole game is: maximise collections, minimise leakage. They're separate problems.

## Why `b` is below your best guess

A charge arrives. You think there's a chance `p` it's genuinely owed.

- Pay it → costs `a`.
- Refuse it → if it *was* owed (chance `p`), you pay it anyway **plus half again** as a lawyer penalty. So refusing costs `1.5a × p` on average.

Refusing only wins when `1.5a·p < a`, i.e. **`p < 2/3`**.

Flip it round: *pay anything you're at least two-thirds sure is legitimate.* So `b` is the price where your confidence falls through 2/3 — and because you carry a *range* for `t`, that lands at the **⅓ point of the range**, noticeably below your best guess. Not timidity: the penalty is 1.5× and the alternative is 1×, so the asymmetry is 3:2 against refusing.

Game 4 says it's working: 240 reviews, **2 penalties totalling €79.50, and zero fraud funded.**

## Why `a` is a cliff, not a slope

This is the part that isn't obvious.

Charge **one euro under `t`** → *every* opponent pays you. All 16. Even the ones who refuse — they pay you anyway, plus their penalty.

Charge **one euro over `t`** → only reviewers whose own limit happens to sit above your price pay. In game 4 that was 2 to 7 out of 16.

So crossing `t` doesn't shave your income. It **divides it by two to eight.**

Game 4 makes it vivid:

| item | our `a` | payers | collected | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 532.50 | **16 / 16** | **8,520** | just under `t` — 55% of our income from one line |
| 2 | 335.00 | 4 / 16 | 1,340 | but `t ≥ 229.50`, so ~230 would have paid **3,672** |

**That single overcharge on item 2 cost about €2,300.**

## So when is charging over `t` right?

Compare the two plays: `16 × (just under t)` versus `your price × payers`. Rearranged, the safe play wins whenever

```
t  >  a × payers / 16
```

- **Item 2**: `335 × 4/16 = 84`. `t` is at least 229 — far above 84. Safe play wins clearly. We got this wrong.
- **Items 5–15**: `t = 0`. Nothing is owed at all, so there *is* no safe play. Every charge is a free lottery ticket, and they paid **€1,690** across 11 lines at zero risk.
- **Item 1**: break-even 232, and `t ∈ [199, 530)`. Genuinely undetermined — could have gone either way.

So the two cases need **opposite** behaviour, and telling them apart *is* the coverage question. That's why `b` collapsing to zero and `a` staying positive on the same line isn't a contradiction — it's the correct response to "worth nothing to me, still worth asking".

## Refinement of what I told you last turn

I said push free shots higher because the acceptance curve looked flat. Game 4 sharpens that: **true only when `t` is actually zero.** On items 1 and 2 — genuinely covered — pushing high cost us money. The lever isn't "how high", it's "is `t` zero or not".

## Where the 9,015 came from

```
income   15,500  =  8,760 fair (items 3, 4)  +  6,740 free shots
cost      6,485  =  6,405 legitimate claims paid  +  79.50 penalties
net       9,015
```

Headroom: placing `a` at the *proven* `t` on every line would have earned **18,040 instead of 15,500** — +2,540, almost all of it item 2, plus item 4 where we charged 15 against `t ≥ 28` (the `K` shading undercharging again).

Two things to tweak, both now measurable from the files you pulled down: stop overcharging covered lines (that's `K`), and stop undercharging the confident ones (also `K`, opposite direction — which is the argument for *fitting* it rather than picking a constant).

content.text:
Now I can answer both parts precisely.

## The rule side

Every line item pairs us with each of 16 opponents **twice** — once as the handyman issuing, once as the insurer reviewing. Each transaction resolves on two yes/no questions:

- **Is the price ≤ `t`?** — fair or inflated. Set by the hidden truth, not by anyone's choice.
- **Is the price ≤ `b`?** — accepted or refused. Set by the insurer.

|  | accepted (`a ≤ b`) | refused (`a > b`) |
|---|---|---|
| **fair** (`a ≤ t`) | H gets `a`, I pays `a` | H gets `a`, **I pays 1.5a** |
| **inflated** (`a > t`) | H gets `min(a,c)`, I pays same | nothing moves |

Read it by role and the asymmetry jumps out:

- **As issuer we're paid in 3 of the 4 cells.** We get nothing only when the price is inflated *and* refused. Our issuer payoff can never be negative.
- **As insurer we pay in 3 of the 4 cells.** We pay nothing only in that same cell. Our insurer payoff can never be positive.

So there are exactly **two ways to gain** and **three ways to lose**:

**Gain 1 — our charge is fair.** All 16 opponents pay, whether they accept or refuse. Refusers pay us *and* eat the penalty. This is the big one.

**Gain 2 — our charge is inflated but under someone's limit.** Only those opponents pay; the rest cost us nothing. Free upside.

**Loss 1 — an opponent's fair charge, we accept.** We pay it. **This is not an error** — it's the cost of doing business. Trying to dodge it converts it into Loss 2 at 1.5× the price.

**Loss 2 — an opponent's fair charge, we refuse.** We pay 1.5×. Error: `b` too low.

**Loss 3 — an opponent's inflated charge, we accept.** We pay it. Error: `b` too high.

The same misplaced `b` produces Loss 2 or Loss 3 depending on which side of `t` it falls, and Loss 2 costs 1.5× while Loss 3 costs 1×. **That 3:2 ratio is the entire reason `b` sits at the ⅓ point of your belief rather than the middle.**

## The amounts — 5 games, 944 transactions each side

| cause | per transaction |
|---|---|
| fair charge collected | **+353** |
| free shot collected | **+121** |
| fair claim paid (unavoidable) | −249 |
| **fair claim refused (penalty)** | **−288** |
| inflated charge rightly refused | 0 |

| | g1 | g2 | g3 | g4 | g5 | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| net | −8,274 | +11,651 | 0 | +9,015 | +1,073 | **+13,465** |

## Game 5 is the cleanest illustration — both errors at once

```
income                                        14,892
  − fair claims we owed and paid               4,621   unavoidable
  − fraud we FUNDED   (items 2,4,5,6,7)        4,272   b too HIGH
  − fair claims we REFUSED (items 8,9,12–15,17) 4,926   b too LOW
                                              ------
net                                            1,073
```

Our income was strong — 14,892, comparable to game 4. **The entire round was eaten by 9,198 of insurer error.** And note it went wrong in *both* directions on different items: `b` too high on five items, too low on seven. That's a **precision** problem, not a bias problem — `mu_shift` cannot fix it, only better `t` estimates can.

Contrast game 2: zero insurer errors, and it netted more (11,651) on *less* income.

## The headline

Across five games we collected **44,608** and paid back **31,142**. Of that outflow:

- ~13,590 was unavoidable — legitimate claims we correctly paid
- **13,280 was wrongful-refusal penalties** (8,274 of it game 1's non-submission, 4,926 game 5)
- **at least 4,272 was fraud we funded** (22 of 29 measured)

**More than half of everything we've paid out was avoidable.** The money is not being lost on the issuing side — that engine works. It's being lost on `b`, and specifically on rounds where the `t` estimates scatter.

content.text:
Straight from the brief ([GAME_DESCRIPTION.md:56](GAME_DESCRIPTION.md#L56)):

- **H** = the **handyman** who issues the invoice — the tradesperson sending the bill. Sets the **charge price `a`**.
- **I** = the **insurance** doing claim handling — reviews the incoming invoice and decides whether to pay. Sets the **acceptance limit `b`**.

The thing that makes it confusing: **we are both, simultaneously, in every matchup.** We submit one `a` and one `b` per line item, and the server pairs us with all 16 opponents twice over:

```
        us as H  →  opponent as I     (our `a` vs their `b`)   → money comes IN
   opponent as H  →  us as I          (their `a` vs our `b`)   → money goes OUT
```

So per line item we're in 32 transactions: 16 where we're the handyman collecting, 16 where we're the insurer paying. That's why 15 items × 16 opponents gave 240 issued + 240 reviewed in game 4.

In the payoff table from the last message, "H gets `a`" means **our income** when we're the issuer, and "I pays 1.5a" means **our cost** when we're the reviewer. Same table, read from two sides — which is why `a` and `b` are optimised against completely different objectives: `a` maximises what H collects, `b` minimises what I leaks.

    tf = R/f"truth_game_{g:02d}.json"

content.text:
Here's what the logs say, and it forces me to correct something I told you earlier.

## Overall: no net bias, but the direction flipped

Across 5 games, **9 items proven under-estimated, 9 proven over-estimated.** But not evenly distributed in time:

| game | under | over | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **8** | 2 | under-shooting |
| 2 | 0 | 1 | |
| 4 | 1 | **4** | over-shooting |
| 6 | 0 | **2** | over-shooting |

**Correction:** last time I told you `K=0.5` was pushing `a` the wrong way, citing "5 of 8 items had `t` above `t_mid`". That was game-1-only data, and every `t_hi` in `truth.py` was `null`, so the test could only *detect* under-estimation. Once I derive upper bounds myself (any charge not paid by all 16 proves `t <` that charge), the recent regime is clearly **over**-estimation. `K=0.5` is defensible; on games 4 and 6 it may not even be enough.

## The stated band contains the truth only 65% of the time

| | count |
|---|---|
| `[t_low, t_high]` brackets the true `t` | 13 / 20 |
| band entirely **above** the truth | 5 |
| band entirely **below** the truth | 2 |

For an interval meant to bracket the answer, 65% is overconfident — and the misses skew high 5:2. Worst cases: game 6 item 1 we said `[1200, 1700]`, truth was `[765, 900)`. Game 6 item 2 we said `[120, 220]`, truth `[0, 45)`.

## Two error modes that need opposite fixes

**A — coverage errors (5 of the 9 over-estimates).** Items nobody ever proved fair, i.e. `t` is very likely 0, where we assigned a positive `t_mid`:

| | our `t_mid` | truth |
|---|---|---|
| g1 item 16 | 220 | `t < 176` |
| g4 item 11 | 150 | `t < 45` |
| g6 item 2 | 170 | `t < 45` |

These aren't pricing errors — the price was irrelevant. Calling a junk line "covered" gives it a positive `b`, and **that is precisely what funds fraud** (4,272 lost in game 5).

**B — genuine price errors (13 items on lines proven worth something).** Game 1 was uniformly too low (1.01–1.44×); games 2/4/6 uniformly too high (1.08–1.67×). Median over-estimate 1.49×, median under-estimate 1.14× — so when we're high, we're *further* wrong.

## The structural point this exposes

**`K` only shades `a`. It does nothing to `b`.** `b` is the ⅓-quantile of the band, so an over-high band produces an over-high `b` regardless of `K` — and that's the exact mechanism behind game 5's 22 funded frauds. Shading the charge cannot fix a mispriced acceptance limit.

Which means the calibration has to move the **band**, not the charge. And a single `mu_shift` won't do it: fitted across all this data it lands near 1.0 — your own `calibration.json` already shows median ratio **1.01**. The level is right; the **variance and the coverage calls** are wrong.

## One thing to check in `calibration.json`

`b_scale: 1.3` scales the acceptance limit *up* by 30%. That makes sense if fitted on game 1, where 27 wrongful rejections dominated. But on games 4–6, where we over-estimate and funded 4,272 of fraud, it pushes the wrong way. Worth re-fitting on games 4–6 only, or splitting it by whether the item's coverage call is confident.

Ranked by measured euros:

1. **Coverage classification** — 5 of 9 over-errors, and the direct cause of funded fraud.
2. **Widen the band** (`sigma_scale` ≈ 1.3–1.5) — 65% coverage says we're overconfident; a wider band lowers `b` on uncertain items.
3. **Re-fit `b_scale` on recent games**, not game 1.
4. `K` — already roughly right for the current regime; leave it.

input.content:
"""Replay a finished round offline and score a strategy against ground truth.

    uv run python -m app.c2f.replay --games 1,2,4,6 --prompt v2

Why this exists: a live round gives one sample of one strategy. Every finished
round, though, is a complete labelled dataset - the transaction feed reveals
every charge and whether it was fair - so a prompt or pricing change can be
scored on real cases before it is ever submitted.

What is exact and what is not:

* **Fairness is exact.** A fair charge is paid by *every* reviewer whether they
  accept or reject, so `paid by all` <=> fair, and `not paid by all` <=> inflated.
  No inference needed.
* **Insurer cost is exact** for every charge whose size we can see.
* **Issuer income is a bracket.** Whether a *new* charge would be accepted
  depends on each opponent's hidden limit, which we only know through the
  inequalities their observed decisions imply. So income is reported as
  [certain, optimistic] rather than a point.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
from collections.abc import Callable, Sequence
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[3]
RUNS = REPO_ROOT / "runs"

#: Which saved log carries real (non-mock) model output for each game.
GAME_LOGS: dict[int, str] = {
    1: "game_01.json",
    2: "dry_game_02.json",
    3: "game_03.json",
    4: "game_04.json",
    6: "game_06.json",
}

WRONGFUL_REJECT_MULTIPLE = 1.5


@dataclass(slots=True)
class Case:
    game_id: int
    policy: str
    description: str
    invoice_text: str
    items: list[dict]
    invoice_meta: dict = field(default_factory=dict)


@dataclass(slots=True)
class Truth:
    """What a finished round proves about each line item."""

    #: item -> largest charge proven fair (t >= this)
    t_lo: dict[int, float]
    #: item -> smallest charge proven inflated (t < this)
    t_hi: dict[int, float]
    #: item -> [(charge, is_fair)] for every charge whose size is visible
    charges: dict[int, list[tuple[float, bool]]]
    #: item -> opponent -> (b_lower, b_upper) implied by their decisions
    limits: dict[int, dict[str, tuple[float, float]]]
    #: charges that nobody paid, so their size is unknowable
    censored: int
    opponents: int


def load_case(game_id: int) -> Case:
    log = json.loads((RUNS / GAME_LOGS[game_id]).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    case = log["case"]
    return Case(
        game_id=game_id,
        policy=case.get("policy", ""),
        description=case.get("description", ""),
        invoice_text=case.get("invoice_text", ""),
        items=case.get("items", []),
        invoice_meta=case.get("invoice_meta", {}),
    )


def saved_estimates(game_id: int) -> dict[int, dict]:
    """The estimates that were actually used in the round, for a baseline."""
    log = json.loads((RUNS / GAME_LOGS[game_id]).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    src = log.get("ensemble") or log.get("model_full", {}).get("output") or {}
    return {int(i["index"]): i for i in src.get("items", [])}


def load_truth(game_id: int, txn_dir: Path, us: str) -> Truth:
    """Reconstruct ground truth from every team's transaction records."""
    per: dict[tuple[int, str], dict[str, tuple[bool, float]]] = {}
    for path in txn_dir.glob(f"g{game_id}_*.json"):
        for row in json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")).get("items", []):
            key = (row["line_item_index"], row["issuer"])
            per.setdefault(key, {})[row["reviewer"]] = (row["accepted"], row["amount"])

    t_lo: dict[int, float] = {}
    t_hi: dict[int, float] = {}
    charges: dict[int, list[tuple[float, bool]]] = {}
    limits: dict[int, dict[str, tuple[float, float]]] = {}
    censored = 0
    opponents: set[str] = set()

    for (item, issuer), revs in sorted(per.items()):
        opponents.update(revs)
        paid = [amount for _acc, amount in revs.values() if amount > 0]
        if not paid:
            # Either the charge was zero (everyone "accepts" it) or it was
            # inflated and refused by all, in which case its size left no trace.
            if any(not acc for acc, _a in revs.values()):
                censored += 1
            continue

        charge = max(paid)
        fair = len(paid) == len(revs)
        if fair:
            t_lo[item] = max(t_lo.get(item, 0.0), charge)
        else:
            t_hi[item] = min(t_hi.get(item, float("inf")), charge)
        if issuer != us:
            charges.setdefault(item, []).append((charge, fair))

        # Every decision on a known charge bounds that reviewer's limit.
        for reviewer, (accepted, _amount) in revs.items():
            if reviewer == us:
                continue
            low, high = limits.setdefault(item, {}).get(reviewer, (0.0, float("inf")))
            if accepted:
                low = max(low, charge)
            else:
                high = min(high, charge)
            limits[item][reviewer] = (low, high)

    opponents.discard(us)
    return Truth(t_lo, t_hi, charges, limits, censored, len(opponents))


def insurer_cost(our_b: dict[int, float], truth: Truth) -> tuple[float, int, int]:
    """Exact cost of our acceptance limits against the charges actually received.

    Returns (cost, fraud_funded_count, fair_refused_count).
    """
    cost = 0.0
    funded = refused = 0
    for item, rows in truth.charges.items():
        limit = our_b.get(item, 0.0)
        for charge, fair in rows:
            if charge <= limit:
                cost += charge
                if not fair:
                    funded += 1
            elif fair:
                cost += WRONGFUL_REJECT_MULTIPLE * charge
                refused += 1
    return cost, funded, refused


def issuer_income(our_a: dict[int, float], truth: Truth) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Bracket on what our charges would collect.

    A charge at or below a proven-fair price is collected from every opponent.
    Above that we can only count opponents whose limit is *provably* high
    enough (certain) or *possibly* high enough (optimistic).
    """
    certain = optimistic = 0.0
    for item, charge in our_a.items():
        if charge <= 0:
            continue
        proven_fair = charge <= truth.t_lo.get(item, 0.0)
        if proven_fair:
            certain += truth.opponents * charge
            optimistic += truth.opponents * charge
            continue

        item_limits = truth.limits.get(item, {})
        sure = sum(1 for low, _high in item_limits.values() if charge <= low)
        maybe = sum(1 for _low, high in item_limits.values() if charge < high)
        unseen = truth.opponents - len(item_limits)
        certain += sure * charge
        optimistic += (maybe + unseen) * charge
    return certain, optimistic


@dataclass(slots=True)
class Score:
    game_id: int
    label: str
    income_certain: float
    income_optimistic: float
    cost: float
    fraud_funded: int
    fair_refused: int

    @property
    def net_certain(self) -> float:
        return self.income_certain - self.cost

    @property
    def net_optimistic(self) -> float:
        return self.income_optimistic - self.cost


def score(
    label: str,
    game_id: int,
    priced: Sequence[dict],
    truth: Truth,
) -> Score:
    a = {int(r["index"]): float(r["charge_price"]) for r in priced}
    b = {int(r["index"]): float(r["acceptance_limit"]) for r in priced}
    cost, funded, refused = insurer_cost(b, truth)
    certain, optimistic = issuer_income(a, truth)
    return Score(game_id, label, certain, optimistic, cost, funded, refused)


PricingFn = Callable[[dict], tuple[float, float]]


def price_all(estimates: dict[int, dict], pricing: PricingFn) -> list[dict]:
    out = []
    for index, est in sorted(estimates.items()):
        charge, limit = pricing(est)
        out.append({"index": index, "charge_price": charge, "acceptance_limit": limit})
    return out

    return {int(i["index"]): i for i in src.get("items", [])}


def load_truth(game_id: int, txn_dir: Path, us: str) -> Truth:
    """Reconstruct ground truth from every team's transaction records."""
    per: dict[tuple[int, str], dict[str, tuple[bool, float]]] = {}
    for path in txn_dir.glob(f"g{game_id}_*.json"):
        for row in json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")).get("items", []):
            key = (row["line_item_index"], row["issuer"])
            per.setdefault(key, {})[row["reviewer"]] = (row["accepted"], row["amount"])

    t_lo: dict[int, float] = {}
    t_hi: dict[int, float] = {}
    charges: dict[int, list[tuple[float, bool]]] = {}
    limits: dict[int, dict[str, tuple[float, float]]] = {}
    censored = 0
    opponents: set[str] = set()

    for (item, issuer), revs in sorted(per.items()):
        opponents.update(revs)
        paid = [amount for _acc, amount in revs.values() if amount > 0]
        if not paid:
            # Either the charge was zero (everyone "accepts" it) or it was
            # inflated and refused by all, in which case its size left no trace.
            if any(not acc for acc, _a in revs.values()):
                censored += 1
            continue

        charge = max(paid)
        fair = len(paid) == len(revs)
        if fair:
            t_lo[item] = max(t_lo.get(item, 0.0), charge)
        else:
            t_hi[item] = min(t_hi.get(item, float("inf")), charge)
        if issuer != us:
            charges.setdefault(item, []).append((charge, fair))

        # Every decision on a known charge bounds that reviewer's limit.
        for reviewer, (accepted, _amount) in revs.items():
            if reviewer == us:
                continue
            low, high = limits.setdefault(item, {}).get(reviewer, (0.0, float("inf")))
            if accepted:
                low = max(low, charge)
            else:
                high = min(high, charge)
            limits[item][reviewer] = (low, high)

    opponents.discard(us)
    return Truth(t_lo, t_hi, charges, limits, censored, len(opponents))


def insurer_cost(our_b: dict[int, float], truth: Truth) -> tuple[float, int, int]:
    """Exact cost of our acceptance limits against the charges actually received.

    Returns (cost, fraud_funded_count, fair_refused_count).
    """
    cost = 0.0
    funded = refused = 0
    for item, rows in truth.charges.items():
        limit = our_b.get(item, 0.0)
        for charge, fair in rows:
            if charge <= limit:
                cost += charge
                if not fair:
                    funded += 1
            elif fair:
                cost += WRONGFUL_REJECT_MULTIPLE * charge
                refused += 1
    return cost, funded, refused


def issuer_income(our_a: dict[int, float], truth: Truth) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Bracket on what our charges would collect.

    A charge at or below a proven-fair price is collected from every opponent.
    Above that we can only count opponents whose limit is *provably* high
    enough (certain) or *possibly* high enough (optimistic).
    """
    certain = optimistic = 0.0
    for item, charge in our_a.items():
        if charge <= 0:
            continue
        proven_fair = charge <= truth.t_lo.get(item, 0.0)
        if proven_fair:
            certain += truth.opponents * charge
            optimistic += truth.opponents * charge
            continue

        item_limits = truth.limits.get(item, {})
        sure = sum(1 for low, _high in item_limits.values() if charge <= low)
        maybe = sum(1 for _low, high in item_limits.values() if charge < high)
        unseen = truth.opponents - len(item_limits)
        certain += sure * charge
        optimistic += (maybe + unseen) * charge
    return certain, optimistic


@dataclass(slots=True)
class Score:
    game_id: int
    label: str
    income_certain: float
    income_optimistic: float
    cost: float
    fraud_funded: int
    fair_refused: int

    @property
    def net_certain(self) -> float:
        return self.income_certain - self.cost

    @property
    def net_optimistic(self) -> float:
        return self.income_optimistic - self.cost


def score(
    label: str,
    game_id: int,
    priced: Sequence[dict],
    truth: Truth,
) -> Score:
    a = {int(r["index"]): float(r["charge_price"]) for r in priced}
    b = {int(r["index"]): float(r["acceptance_limit"]) for r in priced}
    cost, funded, refused = insurer_cost(b, truth)
    certain, optimistic = issuer_income(a, truth)
    return Score(game_id, label, certain, optimistic, cost, funded, refused)


PricingFn = Callable[[dict], tuple[float, float]]


def price_all(estimates: dict[int, dict], pricing: PricingFn) -> list[dict]:
    out = []
    for index, est in sorted(estimates.items()):
        charge, limit = pricing(est)
        out.append({"index": index, "charge_price": charge, "acceptance_limit": limit})
    return out

`t_hi` now resolves: game 4 items 1,2,4 and game 6 both items have real upper bounds where they were all `null` before.

To answer directly — **two ways it helps us:**

1. **Fixing it doubles the labelled data.** Without upper bounds the calibration test is one-sided and can only ever confirm under-estimation. That's why the original diagnosis said "we under-shoot" when games 4–6 actually over-shoot.
2. **A genuinely-null `t_hi` is a signal in itself**: nobody's charge was ever proven inflated on that item, so the ceiling is *untested*. Those are the items where charging higher next time is cheap exploration — as issuer, being wrong costs nothing.

input.content:
"""A second-generation estimation prompt, targeted at measured errors.

Every rule below exists because a specific line item was scored wrong against
recovered ground truth, not because it sounded sensible. The measurements, from
games 1-6:

* Ancillary lines are the worst category by ratio - vehicle costs 40 vs t<28,
  30 vs t<20, diagnostic report 150 vs t<45, call-out 170 vs t<45. Two to four
  times too high.
* Consumer electronics run 1.3-1.7x too high - TV 600 vs t<530, speakers 500 vs
  t<335, TV+speakers 1500 vs t<900.
* Water-damage remediation services run LOW - room drying 420 vs t>=606,
  moisture measurement 160 vs t>=228, leak detection 360 vs t>=410.
* The stated [t_low, t_high] band contained the truth only 65% of the time, and
  missed high 5 times to 2. It is too narrow and centred too high.
* An upgrade line is not worth zero: premium hardwood skirting billed as an
  upgrade still proved t >= 98, because the like-for-like softwood it replaced
  was owed.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

SYSTEM_V2 = """You are a senior German insurance claims expert assessing an invoice \
submitted after an insured event. For EVERY line item you decide coverage and the \
fair gross total.

For each item return:
1. covered - is this TYPE of cost insured? Check insured event, conditions of cover, \
basis of indemnity, and exclusions.
2. related - does it belong to the reported damage?
3. t_low / t_mid / t_high - the gross total for the whole line (quantity x unit price, \
including 19% VAT, EUR) that a frugal claims expert would still accept. t_mid is your \
best estimate of the ceiling.
If not covered or not related: t_low = t_mid = t_high = 0, and put what it WOULD have \
cost into t_if_covered.

BASIS OF INDEMNITY comes first. Find the clause saying what the policy pays - market \
value at time of loss, replacement cost, repair cost, or depreciated value - and apply \
THAT, not the wording of the invoice line. A line reading "New Bike" under a policy \
paying market value at the time of theft is worth the market value, not a new bicycle.

If the documents STATE the amount (a stated worth, appraisal, sum insured, purchase \
price with a date), that figure IS the answer: anchor on it and set all three numbers \
within a few percent of each other.

CALIBRATION RULES, each measured against real outcomes:

- ANCILLARY LINES ARE CHEAP. Call-out, travel, vehicle costs, delivery, disposal, \
administration, handling, diagnostic reports, "inspection" and "assessment" lines: \
claims experts allow very little for these and often absorb them entirely. Unless the \
policy names a higher allowance, keep t_mid under EUR 50 for such a line, even when \
the invoice asks for several hundred.

- CONSUMER ELECTRONICS AND APPLIANCES: price the BUDGET-to-lower-mid model, not the \
mid or premium one, and apply depreciation for age where the policy pays market or \
actual cash value. When in doubt take the low end.

- WATER-DAMAGE REMEDIATION SERVICES ARE NOT CHEAP. Room drying, dehumidifier and fan \
hire, moisture measurement and mapping, leak detection and locating the escape are \
specialist services billed at professional day rates over several days. Do not shade \
these down; they routinely run higher than they look.

- UPGRADES ARE NOT WORTH ZERO. When a line bills a better standard than what was lost \
(natural stone for ceramic, hardwood for softwood, premium for standard), the upgrade \
itself is not owed but the LIKE-FOR-LIKE replacement of the damaged original IS. Set \
t to the cost of restoring the pre-loss standard, not to zero and not to the upgrade \
price. Only a line that is purely precautionary, purely maintenance, or aimed at an \
item the loss never reached is worth zero.

- EXCLUDED INSTALLATIONS: repairing an excluded installation (pool plant, \
photovoltaics) is worth zero, but the damage its escape caused to insured property is \
fully covered, and locating the escape is covered either way.

BAND WIDTH. t_low and t_high must genuinely bracket the answer - they are wrong about \
a third of the time when they are drawn tight. Unless the documents state the amount, \
make t_high at least 1.6x t_low, and wider still for a vague description or an item \
type you are unsure about. A wide honest band is worth more than a narrow confident \
one: it is used to decide what we refuse to pay, and overconfidence there is what \
funds fraud.

Answer with ONLY a JSON object of this exact shape, no markdown fences:

{
  "policy_summary": "one line: what is insured, main limits/exclusions",
  "items": [
    {
      "index": 1,
      "covered": true,
      "related": true,
      "clause": "policy clause relied on",
      "basis": "basis of indemnity applied",
      "t_low": 380,
      "t_mid": 420,
      "t_high": 700,
      "t_if_covered": 0,
      "reason": "max 12 words"
    }
  ]

content.text:
There are **two different reasons**, and only one was our bug.

## Reason 1 — our algorithm threw the information away (games 4, 6)

`truth.py` infers `t` only from the aggregated per-pair matchup cells. Look at the discriminating function:

```python
def _diff(a, acc, t):
    if a <= t: return 2*a if acc else 2.5*a
    return     2*a if acc else 0.0
```

**An accepted charge contributes `2a` whether it was fair or inflated — identical.** So accepted charges carry *zero* information in that method. Only *rejections* discriminate (`2.5a` fair vs `0` inflated), and even those arrive only as one aggregate sum per team pair, which then has to be disentangled across every item in the case simultaneously — a subset-sum problem the code attacks with meet-in-the-middle search.

With many items that system is underdetermined, so lots of candidate intervals survive, including the topmost one `[max_charge, ∞)`. And [truth.py:148](c2f/truth.py#L148) emits `t_hi = None` exactly when that top interval is still feasible.

What it never used is the one thing that identifies fairness outright: **who paid**. A fair charge is paid by *every* reviewer; an inflated one only by those who accepted. That's visible per transaction in the `amount` field — no aggregation, no disentangling. Game 4 item 1 had **8 visible inflated charges** sitting right there in the data, and the pair algebra couldn't see any of them.

That's what the patch fixed: game 4 items 1, 2, 4 and both game 6 items now have real upper bounds.

## Reason 2 — genuinely no evidence exists (most of game 1)

Game 1 is different, and my patch correctly leaves those `null`:

| item | visible fair | visible inflated | size-hidden |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3 | **0** | 14 |
| 2 | 4 | **0** | 13 |
| 6 | 4 | **0** | 13 |
| 7 | 4 | **0** | 13 |

**No inflated charge was ever visible on those items.** 13–14 of the 17 charges were size-hidden — teams that submitted nothing, so their charge was 0 and left no trace. With no charge ever proven inflated, no upper bound exists in the data at all. That's honest missing information, not a bug, and no algorithm can recover it.

It'll resolve on its own: either someone overcharges that item type in a future round, or we probe upward ourselves — which costs nothing as issuer.

## So, to answer directly

Not the platform, and not the API. It was our inference method discarding the strongest signal in the feed. Roughly half the nulls were recoverable and now are; the rest are real gaps concentrated in game 1, where almost nobody submitted.

I stopped short of running the prompt A/B — say the word and I'll continue, now against meaningfully better ground truth than before.
